what-is-an-operating-system.title: Abstraction, isolation, and multiplexing
what-is-an-operating-system.body: A CPU runs instructions, but it does not understand files, users, or applications. The OS builds those abstractions from hardware mechanisms. A process receives a virtual address space; a descriptor names an open resource; a scheduler divides CPU time. Isolation requires both hardware permissions and correct kernel checks. Multiplexing is the reuse of one physical resource by several logical owners.

what-is-an-operating-system.title: Worked example: one CPU, three applications
what-is-an-operating-system.body: Suppose an editor needs 2 ms of CPU and then waits 10 ms for storage. A player needs 1 ms every 5 ms to replenish audio. Running the editor until its I/O finishes would waste the CPU and delay playback. Blocking the editor and scheduling the player allows useful overlap. This is concurrency; simultaneous execution would require another execution unit. The policy must also prevent a third CPU-heavy process from starving the player.

what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.title: From pathname to execution
what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.body: The shell resolves the command and arranges input, output, and environment. On a typical Unix path it creates a child, which calls execve. The kernel validates the executable, replaces mappings, and prepares arguments and auxiliary metadata. A dynamic loader resolves required libraries before language startup calls main. A failed exec returns an error to the existing process instead of magically creating a running program.

what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.title: Demand loading and termination
what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.body: Mapping a 20 MiB executable does not require reading all 20 MiB immediately. First instruction and data accesses can fault pages into RAM. When main returns, runtime cleanup precedes the exit system call; the kernel closes descriptors and retains waitable status. Compare a cold launch and warm launch separately: the second may benefit from cached file pages without changing program semantics.

course-environment.title: A reproducible experiment
course-environment.body: Use a disposable Linux environment and record uname -a, compiler version, and whether the process is inside a VM or container. Save source and exact build flags together. Start with one variable: compare a single-threaded program with a two-threaded version using identical inputs. Repeat timings, because page-cache state, CPU frequency, and other processes affect results.

course-environment.title: Interpreting the environment
course-environment.body: A container shares the host kernel, while a VM runs a guest kernel. Therefore a missing syscall cannot be fixed merely by changing a container's user-space packages. WSL behavior depends on its architecture and integration with Windows. Keep exercise files in a dedicated directory and bound memory, thread counts, and execution time so an experiment measures the intended mechanism rather than exhausting the machine.

c-survival-guide-for-os.title: Pointers, lengths, and ownership
c-survival-guide-for-os.body: Represent a buffer with both its address and capacity. A pointer may refer to a stack object, static storage, or a heap allocation, and each has a different lifetime. Passing a stack address to a worker that outlives the function is invalid even if the bytes appear unchanged. Ownership answers who releases an allocation; borrowing answers how long another function may access it.

c-survival-guide-for-os.title: Partial I/O example
c-survival-guide-for-os.body: If read(fd, buf, 16) returns 5, only buf[0] through buf[4] contain newly read bytes. A return of zero indicates end-of-file for an ordinary stream read; a negative return indicates failure. A loop must accumulate progress, handle interruption according to the API contract, and avoid retrying a permanent error forever. Writing 16 bytes after reading 5 can leak stale buffer contents. Text termination requires separate capacity and explicit handling.

essential-system-tools.title: Choose an observation before a command
essential-system-tools.body: Use ps to identify a process, top to see changing CPU use, and vmstat to distinguish runnable demand from blocked work. Use ss for socket state and iostat for device observations when available. strace answers which system calls occurred, not why application code chose them. Sampling a CPU profile answers where on-CPU time went, not which remote dependency consumed wall time.

essential-system-tools.title: Compare rates and intervals
essential-system-tools.body: A counter increasing from 1,000 to 1,600 in 10 seconds means 60 events per second. Compare that rate against completed requests during the same interval. If requests fall while retries rise, additional system activity may represent wasted work. Repeat a baseline and a changed configuration with equal workloads; retain timestamps so process, application, and device measurements can be correlated.

how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.title: Architectural state versus implementation
how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.body: The instruction set specifies observable register and memory effects. Internally, a CPU may pipeline decoding, predict branches, and execute independent operations before earlier ones finish. Retirement preserves the required architectural behavior. A long dependent load chain cannot exploit the same parallelism as several independent loads because the address of the next load is not yet known.

how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.title: Worked comparison
how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.body: In an array sum, adjacent elements often share cache lines and hardware prefetching can anticipate access. In a pointer-linked list, each node reveals the next address only after its load completes. Both algorithms visit n elements, yet the list can take much longer. Measure cycles and cache misses across multiple runs; source-code line count is not an execution-cost model.

privilege-levels.title: Authority belongs to the kernel
privilege-levels.body: User code cannot install arbitrary page-table mappings or directly control protected devices. A trap enters a known handler with defined saved state. The handler interprets syscall arguments, validates user pointers, and checks the caller's identity. Kernel execution on behalf of a user is still constrained by that user's permitted operation; entering privileged mode is not an authorization grant.

privilege-levels.title: Mode switch versus task switch
privilege-levels.body: If getpid completes immediately, execution may enter and leave the kernel while the same task stays scheduled. If read must wait for disk, the kernel can block the caller and schedule another task. The first is a privilege transition; the second additionally changes scheduled execution context. Counting syscalls as context switches therefore gives the wrong performance diagnosis.

the-memory-hierarchy.title: Locality and cache lines
the-memory-hierarchy.body: Temporal locality reuses a recently accessed item; spatial locality uses nearby items brought in with it. A cache line is the transfer unit between levels, so using one byte may fetch neighboring bytes too. Associativity and replacement policy influence which lines survive. Capacity misses, conflicts, and coherence traffic are distinct reasons a useful line might be unavailable.

the-memory-hierarchy.title: A concrete traversal
the-memory-hierarchy.body: For a row-major matrix, traversing consecutive columns within one row usually consumes nearby addresses. Traversing one column across many rows jumps by a row stride. If that stride repeatedly lands on different pages or conflicting cache sets, identical arithmetic produces more stalls. Blocking the matrix into tiles can retain a working region in cache, at the cost of more complicated loop structure.

interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.title: Cause and restart behavior
interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.body: A device interrupt reports an asynchronous event such as receive completion. An exception arises while executing an instruction, such as a division error or failed address translation. A deliberate trap requests a controlled service. Whether an instruction is retried, skipped, or terminates execution depends on the architecture and event; these events are not interchangeable merely because each enters a handler.

interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.title: Following a demand fault
interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.body: A load touches a valid mapped page that is not resident. The handler checks the region, arranges a frame and any necessary I/O, updates translation state, and resumes the faulting instruction. If the same address lies outside every valid region, allocating memory would hide a bug; the OS instead reports an invalid access. A recoverable fault may still block long enough to affect request latency.

what-the-kernel-manages.title: Objects and references
what-the-kernel-manages.body: A task points to an address space, credentials, descriptor table, and scheduling state. A descriptor table entry refers to an open file description or another kernel object. Multiple tasks may share some of those objects while owning others independently. This graph of references explains why closing one descriptor does not necessarily destroy the underlying resource.

what-the-kernel-manages.title: Resource accounting
what-the-kernel-manages.body: A server's memory includes user allocations, stacks, mapped pages, and kernel-side buffers. Opening sockets consumes more than integer descriptor slots. Increasing an application concurrency limit can therefore exhaust kernel resources before the heap reaches its configured maximum. Diagnose the specific exhausted object and its lifecycle instead of treating every failure as a lack of RAM.

kernel-architectures.title: Where services execute
kernel-architectures.body: A monolithic kernel places major services in privileged kernel space, allowing direct internal calls. A microkernel moves more services into isolated processes and communicates through messages. Hybrid designs combine choices rather than occupying a precise middle point. Modules can make a monolithic kernel extensible without turning those modules into isolated user processes.

kernel-architectures.title: Failure and performance trade-offs
kernel-architectures.body: Moving a driver out of the kernel can limit the damage from its crash, but adds communication and scheduling boundaries. Keeping it inside can reduce call overhead while enlarging the trusted failure domain. Compare concrete paths: how many messages, copies, privilege transitions, and recovery steps does one I/O operation need? Architecture names alone do not determine speed or reliability.

system-calls.title: The API boundary
system-calls.body: A library wrapper packages arguments in the platform's syscall convention, enters the kernel, and translates results into its language interface. The kernel treats all user-controlled pointers, lengths, paths, and flags as untrusted. Validation includes authorization and consistency, not merely checking that an address is nonzero. API contracts define which partial effects can occur before an error.

system-calls.title: Library calls are not syscall counts
system-calls.body: printf may format into a user-space buffer and make no immediate write syscall. A later flush can combine many calls into one write. Conversely one library operation can trigger several kernel operations. Use a trace to distinguish formatting time, buffering, kernel entry, and blocking. Batching reduces boundary overhead but may delay when output becomes visible.

inside-a-system-call.title: Entry, dispatch, and return
inside-a-system-call.body: The CPU switches to a defined entry path, the kernel saves required state, and dispatch selects the implementation. The implementation validates arguments and performs or queues the operation. Before returning, the kernel may process pending work such as signals. The return convention communicates a value or error to the wrapper, which restores the user-facing interface.

inside-a-system-call.title: Fast and blocking paths
inside-a-system-call.body: A read satisfied from cached pages can copy bytes and return without waiting for storage. A cache miss may enqueue I/O and put the task to sleep. Both calls have the same API, yet radically different latency. Separate time spent executing kernel code from time spent descheduled; adding CPU capacity will not remove a slow device wait.

boot-elf-and-the-abi.title: Bootstrapping layers
boot-elf-and-the-abi.body: Firmware selects a boot path, a bootloader loads a kernel, and the kernel initializes enough memory and devices to start user space. The first user-space service then starts other services. Details differ across platforms; the essential dependency is that each stage establishes the environment required by the next. A running shell is near the end of that sequence, not the boot mechanism itself.

boot-elf-and-the-abi.title: Executable format versus calling convention
boot-elf-and-the-abi.body: ELF describes segments, symbols, and metadata needed to load a program on relevant Unix platforms. An ABI also defines register use, stack alignment, argument passing, and binary interfaces. Two functions with the same source signature can still be incompatible if compiled against different conventions. Dynamic linking additionally requires compatible symbol names and versions; merely finding a library file is insufficient.

linux-windows-and-macos.title: Comparable concepts, different contracts
linux-windows-and-macos.body: All three platforms provide processes, virtual memory, files, and protected kernel services, but their object models and APIs differ. Unix descriptors and Windows handles are not identical. Linux epoll reports readiness, while Windows IOCP reports completion. Porting requires preserving the intended operation and lifecycle, not replacing function names mechanically.

linux-windows-and-macos.title: A portability exercise
linux-windows-and-macos.body: Write down what a server assumes about path syntax, case sensitivity, signal delivery, thread cancellation, and socket closure. Then identify which assumptions belong to a language runtime and which require native APIs. Test shutdown while requests are active: a program that works on the happy path can still leak handles or lose output when its platform's termination behavior differs.

program-vs-process.title: Code is a recipe; a process is an execution
program-vs-process.body: An executable file contains instructions and static metadata. A process combines those instructions with a current instruction pointer, registers, address mappings, credentials, and references to open resources. Starting the same executable twice creates two executions with independent lifetimes. Their read-only code pages can still share physical storage without making their mutable application variables shared.

program-vs-process.title: Example: two copies of a counter
program-vs-process.body: Launch two programs whose variable starts at zero. Incrementing the first program's variable does not increment the second, even when a debugger displays the same virtual address in both. Each address is interpreted in its own address space. Explicit shared memory or another IPC mechanism is necessary to coordinate their counters; identical program text is not a communication channel.

the-process-control-block.title: The kernel's execution record
the-process-control-block.body: The textbook process control block groups the information needed to manage execution: identity, state, saved registers, scheduling metadata, accounting, and references to memory and files. Real kernels distribute these responsibilities among linked structures. A task record should therefore be understood as an entry point into an object graph, not as a copy of every byte the process owns.

the-process-control-block.title: Example: suspending and resuming a worker
the-process-control-block.body: A worker blocks while reading a socket. The kernel records where execution can resume and attaches the task to an appropriate wait mechanism. Its memory mappings and open socket remain alive. When data arrives, the task becomes runnable; only after a scheduler selects it do the saved context and kernel continuation actually resume. Waking and running are separate events.

process-states.title: Runnable, running, and blocked
process-states.body: Running means a CPU is executing the task now. Runnable means the task could execute but is waiting for CPU service. Blocked means an event, such as data availability or a lock release, must occur first. A timer may move a running task back to the runnable queue; an I/O completion moves a blocked task to runnable, not directly onto a CPU.

process-states.title: Example: latency with an idle CPU
process-states.body: A request spends 2 ms computing, 40 ms waiting for storage, and 3 ms runnable behind other work. Its elapsed time is 45 ms even though it uses only 2 ms of CPU. More cores might reduce the 3 ms queue delay but cannot remove the 40 ms device wait. Diagnose state durations before selecting a performance fix.

fork-exec-wait-exit.title: Separate creation, replacement, and collection
fork-exec-wait-exit.body: fork creates a child execution; exec replaces a program image; wait collects a child's termination status; exit ends execution. Treating these as one operation hides important failure paths. The child must handle a failed exec, and the parent must eventually collect children it is responsible for. A shell also arranges descriptor redirection before starting the requested program.

fork-exec-wait-exit.title: Example: why output can appear twice
fork-exec-wait-exit.body: Buffered output created before a fork can exist in both processes' user-space buffers afterward. If each process later flushes that buffer, the same text can be emitted twice even though the original print statement ran once. Flush deliberately before creation when appropriate, and use the correct child failure path after exec fails. Also close unused pipe ends so readers can observe end-of-file.

clone-and-what-fork-shares.title: Sharing is a set of choices
clone-and-what-fork-shares.body: Linux task creation can select which resources are shared, such as address space, descriptor table, and signal-handler configuration. Thread creation uses a coordinated combination of these choices rather than merely changing a task's name. Sharing an address space lets tasks see the same allocations, but each running thread still needs its own execution context and stack discipline.

clone-and-what-fork-shares.title: Example: descriptor table versus open object
clone-and-what-fork-shares.body: Two tasks can have separate descriptor tables whose entries reference the same open file description, or they can share the descriptor table itself. In the first case closing one entry does not remove the other's entry, although file offsets may be shared. In the second, table mutations are visible to both. Always identify which layer is shared before predicting behavior.

zombies-and-orphans.title: Termination does not finish the parent's bookkeeping
zombies-and-orphans.body: A zombie has stopped executing and released ordinary execution resources, but retains enough information for its parent to collect an exit status. It is not consuming CPU in an endless loop. An orphan is a child whose parent has exited; it may still be running. Adoption and reaping behavior depends on the process hierarchy, including subreapers and PID namespaces.

zombies-and-orphans.title: Example: a supervisor that never waits
zombies-and-orphans.body: A supervisor launches a short-lived child every second but never collects results. Child execution ends normally while retained termination records accumulate. Killing an already terminated child cannot solve this leak. The supervisor must reap children and handle bursts of exits correctly, rather than assuming one signal corresponds to exactly one terminated child. Design shutdown and error paths to reap as well.

context-switching.title: Direct work and indirect disruption
context-switching.body: A switch preserves one execution context and restores another. Depending on the tasks and architecture, it may also change memory-translation context and other CPU state. Direct register bookkeeping is only part of the cost. The incoming task may need instructions and data that displaced the previous task's useful cache working set.

context-switching.title: Example: more workers can reduce throughput
context-switching.body: Suppose eight CPU-heavy workers compete on two available CPUs. Adding another hundred workers does not create CPU capacity. It can increase runnable waiting, scheduler work, and cache churn. Measure completions, runnable delay, and switches together. A high switch count can also reflect productive I/O concurrency, so the counter alone does not prove a problem or justify reducing concurrency.

signals.title: Notification with restricted execution context
signals.body: A signal can request termination, report a fault, or notify a process of an event. Disposition determines whether the default action, a handler, or ignoring applies; masks control delivery to threads. Handlers interrupt normal control flow, so calling arbitrary library functions from them can deadlock or corrupt state. Use the platform's async-signal-safe operations or defer work to normal execution.

signals.title: Example: graceful shutdown
signals.body: On a termination request, record a shutdown flag or notify the main event loop through a suitable mechanism. Stop accepting new work, finish bounded in-flight operations, and close resources in ordinary code. Do not perform complex logging, allocation, and mutex-heavy cleanup inside the handler. Standard signals may coalesce, so use durable state rather than treating deliveries as a reliable event count.

process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.title: Organizing a terminal workload
process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.body: A process group collects related processes, often the members of a shell pipeline. A session groups process groups and may own a controlling terminal. The foreground process group receives terminal-generated signals. These relationships are independent of whether a process is currently scheduled, and they are more expressive than assuming every child should receive every signal sent to its parent.

process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.title: Example: stopping a pipeline
process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.body: For a command pipeline, the shell arranges the participating commands into a job. Pressing the terminal interrupt key targets the foreground group, allowing all pipeline members to react. A background job is a different group, not a lower-priority CPU class. A robust shell tracks group state and waits for all relevant children before declaring a job fully completed.

why-scheduling-exists.title: CPU service is a shared resource
why-scheduling-exists.body: Runnable tasks compete for a finite number of execution slots. Scheduling selects who runs, for how long, and on which CPU. The objective depends on workload: interactive responsiveness, batch throughput, fairness, or deadline compliance. A policy that maximizes total work can still produce unacceptable pauses for a user-facing task, so there is no universal best ordering.

why-scheduling-exists.title: Example: overlap computation with waiting
why-scheduling-exists.body: Task A computes for 3 ms and blocks for 20 ms; task B has 10 ms of independent CPU work. Scheduling B while A waits uses time that would otherwise be idle. When A becomes ready, preemption policy determines its response delay. This overlap improves utilization on one CPU without allowing the two instruction streams to execute simultaneously.

scheduling-metrics.title: Measure the right interval
scheduling-metrics.body: Turnaround is completion time minus arrival time. Response time is first execution time minus arrival time. Waiting time measures runnable time without CPU service; blocked time is separate. Throughput counts completions per interval, while utilization measures occupied capacity. Means hide outliers, so include latency distributions and distinguish a process-level CPU metric from the user's end-to-end request latency.

scheduling-metrics.title: Worked calculation
scheduling-metrics.body: A CPU-only job arrives at time 2, first runs at 5, uses 4 time units, and finishes at 11 after preemption. Its turnaround is 9, response is 3, and total runnable waiting is 5. If it instead includes 2 units blocked on I/O, waiting becomes 3. Subtracting only CPU time from turnaround is valid only when other states are accounted for.

fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.title: Ordering and preemption
fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.body: First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preemption. Shortest-job-first chooses the smallest available CPU burst but needs a prediction of that duration. Shortest-remaining-time-first can preempt when a newly available job has less work remaining. Short-job policies can reduce average waiting while making a long job wait repeatedly under a stream of short arrivals.

fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.title: Worked schedule
fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.body: Let A and B arrive at time 0 with bursts of 8 and 2, and C arrive at time 1 with burst 1. FCFS with A first completes A at 8, B at 10, and C at 11. Nonpreemptive SJF starts B, then C, then A, completing at 2, 3, and 11. Record the arrival assumptions and tie-break rule; otherwise two apparently conflicting schedules may both be valid.

round-robin.title: The quantum controls a trade-off
round-robin.body: Round robin rotates runnable tasks after a bounded quantum. A short quantum improves opportunities to respond but creates more switch overhead. A very long quantum approaches first-come behavior for short bursts. Blocking tasks normally leave the runnable rotation until their event completes. Fair turns are not necessarily equal useful work when tasks have different cache behavior or CPU requirements.

round-robin.title: Worked schedule
round-robin.body: With all jobs arriving at zero, bursts A=5, B=3, C=1 and quantum 2 produce A:0–2, B:2–4, C:4–5, A:5–7, B:7–8, A:8–9, ignoring switch cost. Completion times are 9, 8, and 5. Change the quantum to 1 and recompute response and completion times. Then insert a fixed switch cost to see why smaller slices are not free.

priority-scheduling-and-aging.title: Urgency and starvation
priority-scheduling-and-aging.body: A priority scheduler favors higher-ranked runnable tasks. Static priorities are easy to reason about but can indefinitely delay low-priority work if higher-priority demand never stops. Aging increases waiting tasks' effective priority over time, providing a path toward service. The implementation must define whether aging resets after execution and how equal-priority tasks share CPU time.

priority-scheduling-and-aging.title: Example: maintenance behind requests
priority-scheduling-and-aging.body: A server gives interactive requests priority over cleanup. During sustained traffic the cleanup never runs, so temporary files accumulate until requests fail too. Aging or a reserved service budget can keep background work progressing. Do not confuse this starvation problem with priority inversion: inversion involves a high-priority task waiting for a resource held by lower-priority work.

multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.title: Fixed classification versus feedback
multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.body: Multilevel queues divide work into classes with different scheduling rules. A feedback queue additionally moves tasks according to observed behavior. Tasks using a full quantum may move to a lower queue, while short interactive bursts can remain responsive. Periodic priority boosts help prevent starvation. Actual rules must account for total CPU use so tasks cannot game classification by yielding just before expiration.

multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.title: Example: interactive and CPU-heavy jobs
multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.body: A text editor frequently waits for input, whereas a compiler consumes long CPU bursts. A feedback policy can give the editor quick service without making the compiler permanently ineligible. Track cumulative service across voluntary yields: otherwise a compute task can pretend to be interactive. Compare queue transitions over several bursts, not just the first scheduling decision.

multiprocessor-scheduling.title: Placement affects locality
multiprocessor-scheduling.body: Multiple CPUs introduce a placement decision in addition to ordering. Per-CPU queues reduce shared-queue contention, but balancing may move tasks between CPUs. Migration can lose cache warmth and change memory locality. Affinity narrows eligible CPUs; it does not guarantee exclusive access. Simultaneous multithreading also means two logical CPUs can share important physical-core resources.

multiprocessor-scheduling.title: Example: an uneven machine
multiprocessor-scheduling.body: Four workers are pinned to one CPU while three others are idle. Aggregate utilization looks low even though the workers experience a saturated run queue. Relaxing affinity may help, but moving a memory-heavy task far from its NUMA-local pages can add access latency. Inspect allowed CPUs, per-CPU demand, and memory placement before treating balancing as a purely numerical problem.

real-time-scheduling.title: A deadline is a correctness constraint
real-time-scheduling.body: Real-time scheduling reasons about completing work before deadlines, not merely running quickly on average. Hard deadlines cannot tolerate misses; soft deadlines permit degraded value. Fixed-priority and earliest-deadline policies require assumptions about execution cost, periods, blocking, and preemption. Admission control prevents accepting a workload whose required service exceeds available capacity under the model.

real-time-scheduling.title: Worked utilization check
real-time-scheduling.body: For independent periodic tasks with execution/period pairs 1/5 and 2/10, utilization is 0.2+0.2=0.4. That leaves capacity in a simplified single-CPU model, but does not prove every real system will meet deadlines: interrupts, locks, nonpreemptible work, and underestimated execution cost matter. State assumptions before applying a utilization bound, and measure worst-case behavior rather than substituting average runtime.

linux-scheduling-classes.title: Policy names express different contracts
linux-scheduling-classes.body: Linux distinguishes ordinary fair scheduling from real-time policies such as FIFO and round robin and from deadline scheduling. A real-time task can outrank ordinary work even when ordinary tasks have waited a long time. Nice values adjust relative weighting within the appropriate ordinary policy; they do not turn a process into a deadline-guaranteed task.

linux-scheduling-classes.title: Example: a busy high-priority thread
linux-scheduling-classes.body: A high-priority FIFO thread that never blocks can prevent lower-priority work from progressing on an eligible CPU, subject to configured controls. That includes the work needed to service the application itself. Test scheduling changes in a bounded environment and verify runtime limits. Kernel configuration, available policies, privilege checks, and container limits influence what is actually permitted.

fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.title: Virtual service and eligibility
fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.body: Fair scheduling tracks service relative to a task's weight rather than assigning every task identical elapsed slices. CFS organized decisions around virtual runtime. EEVDF adds eligibility based on whether a task is owed service and selects an eligible task with an early virtual deadline. The distinction allows responsiveness to be considered while retaining a model of fair long-term allocation.

fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.title: Reason through a weighted example
fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.body: If two continuously runnable tasks have weights in a 2:1 ratio on one CPU, their long-run service target is roughly two thirds and one third, not equal halves. A newly waking task also needs a fair treatment of prior service. A short slice can improve responsiveness without granting unlimited extra CPU. Verify the running kernel's implementation before assuming a textbook CFS trace describes current behavior.

what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.title: Execution identity and shared ownership
what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.body: A kernel-scheduled thread has registers, a stack, scheduling state, and a thread identity. Threads in one process usually share the address space and many resource references. This sharing is why one thread can pass an allocation to another, but it is also why an invalid write can damage the entire application. Scheduling independence does not imply memory isolation.

what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.title: Example: a blocked worker
what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.body: When one thread waits for a socket, another kernel thread in the same process may execute. They can simultaneously access shared heap objects on separate CPUs. A stack variable is not automatically inaccessible to other threads if its address escapes; its lifetime and synchronization still matter. Distinguish the convention of private stack ownership from hardware-enforced address-space protection.

processes-vs-threads.title: Isolation changes the failure boundary
processes-vs-threads.body: Processes provide separate address spaces by default, which makes accidental cross-process memory corruption harder. Threads make sharing cheap but put correctness responsibility on synchronization and ownership rules. IPC between processes introduces serialization, copying, or shared-memory coordination. Compare recovery needs and data-sharing patterns rather than choosing solely from the slogan that threads are lighter.

processes-vs-threads.title: Example: plugin execution
processes-vs-threads.body: An untrusted or unstable plugin inside a thread can corrupt the host heap or terminate the process. Running it in a separate process creates a stronger crash boundary and permits restart, but the protocol must handle partial messages, deadlines, and plugin failure. Shared memory can improve throughput while reintroducing some shared-state complexity; it does not erase the process boundary's other benefits.

user-and-kernel-threads.title: Who makes the scheduling decision?
user-and-kernel-threads.body: A runtime can schedule many logical tasks onto fewer kernel threads. The kernel sees runnable carrier threads, while the runtime sees its own task queues. This reduces per-task overhead but makes blocking behavior important: a blocking call can occupy a carrier unless the runtime parks, replaces, or otherwise compensates for it. Mapping models vary by runtime and operation.

user-and-kernel-threads.title: Example: one carrier, many tasks
user-and-kernel-threads.body: A cooperative runtime has one kernel thread and a thousand logical tasks. If one task performs long CPU work without yielding, the other tasks cannot progress even when the OS would happily schedule another kernel thread. Async I/O helps with waiting, not CPU computation. Offload bounded CPU work or provide more carriers according to the runtime's model.

thread-creation-and-teardown.title: Creation is only the start of a lifecycle
thread-creation-and-teardown.body: A new thread needs a stack, runtime bookkeeping, and a start routine with valid arguments. The parent must not free or reuse those arguments before the child finishes reading them. Joinable threads require joining to collect completion and release relevant resources; detached threads need another reliable ownership strategy. Cancellation must not abandon locked resources or half-updated invariants.

thread-creation-and-teardown.title: Example: a loop-variable bug
thread-creation-and-teardown.body: A loop starts workers and gives each the address of the same changing loop variable. Workers can observe later values rather than their intended index. Give each worker stable per-worker input and keep it alive until the worker no longer needs it. During shutdown, stop new submissions, signal existing workers, and join them before destroying their shared queue or synchronization objects.

what-a-context-switch-costs.title: Costs depend on what changes
what-a-context-switch-costs.body: Switching between threads sharing an address space may avoid some address-space changes, but still requires execution-state bookkeeping and scheduler work. Cache, translation, and branch-prediction effects can dominate the direct path. A task with a large working set may recover slowly after displacement. There is no single nanosecond constant that accurately describes every switch on every machine.

what-a-context-switch-costs.title: Example: interpreting a benchmark
what-a-context-switch-costs.body: A ping-pong test between two threads includes synchronization, wake-up, scheduling, and communication costs, not just saving registers. Place threads on the same CPU and on different CPUs to expose different paths, but record affinity and workload. Use the result to compare a specific design under stated conditions; do not present it as the universal hardware cost of a context switch.

thread-pools-and-sizing.title: Bound work, not only workers
thread-pools-and-sizing.body: A pool amortizes thread creation and limits simultaneously executing tasks. A queue separates admission from execution; if it is unbounded, the pool can still consume unlimited memory and build extreme latency. Choose queue limits, rejection behavior, timeouts, and shutdown rules alongside worker count. Separate workloads that can block each other, such as CPU jobs and slow external calls.

thread-pools-and-sizing.title: Worked sizing estimate
thread-pools-and-sizing.body: With four usable CPUs, a task using 5 ms CPU and waiting 15 ms has a rough saturation estimate of 4×(1+15/5)=16 workers, assuming independent waits and no other bottleneck. This is a starting hypothesis, not a guarantee. A database allowing only six concurrent queries or a strict memory limit may require fewer. Measure throughput and tail latency as concurrency changes.

runtime-threading-models.title: Language tasks do not all mean OS threads
runtime-threading-models.body: A language may expose native threads, virtual threads, coroutines, or async tasks. These abstractions differ in scheduling, suspension, cancellation, and interaction with blocking native calls. Runtime garbage collection and safepoints can also affect progress. Understand the particular runtime version and APIs instead of inferring kernel behavior from an object named Thread or Task.

runtime-threading-models.title: Example: asynchronous versus parallel
runtime-threading-models.body: An async web handler can suspend while waiting for a response without occupying a dedicated thread for the entire wait. That does not make a CPU-heavy loop parallel or preemptible by other logical tasks on the same event loop. Use a bounded executor for expensive computation where appropriate, and propagate cancellation and deadlines so abandoned requests do not keep consuming capacity.

race-conditions-and-atomicity.title: An operation can contain several visible steps
race-conditions-and-atomicity.body: Incrementing a shared counter conceptually reads, computes, and writes. Two threads can both read 10, both compute 11, and both write 11, losing one increment. Atomic read-modify-write operations make that particular update indivisible, but do not automatically protect a multi-variable invariant. In languages such as C and C++, unsynchronized data races can invalidate ordinary reasoning through undefined behavior.

race-conditions-and-atomicity.title: Example: transferring a balance
race-conditions-and-atomicity.body: Moving 10 units from account A to B must preserve the sum and avoid overdraft. Making each balance atomic does not make the combined check-and-transfer atomic. Use a lock covering the invariant, a correct transaction, or a carefully designed compare-and-swap protocol. Specify a consistent lock order when multiple accounts are involved, and test interleavings around validation as well as updates.

memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.title: Visibility, ordering, and cache ownership
memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.body: An atomic flag can coordinate publication only when its ordering establishes the required relationship with the published data. Release/acquire synchronization is one common pattern; a relaxed atomic alone does not publish unrelated writes. False sharing is different: independent variables occupy the same cache line and cause coherence traffic even though the program has no logical data dependency between them.

memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.title: Example: two per-thread counters
memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.body: Two workers repeatedly update separate counters stored next to each other. If both lie in one cache line, ownership can bounce between cores on each write. Padding or separating hot data may improve throughput, at the cost of memory and cache capacity. First verify the access pattern and actual contention; padding every object can make locality worse rather than better.

mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.title: Different primitives protect different facts
mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.body: A mutex gives one owner exclusive access to an invariant. A semaphore counts available permits and can allow several participants. A condition variable allows waiting for a predicate protected by a mutex; it is not a queue of durable notifications. Waiting releases the mutex atomically with entering the wait protocol and reacquires it before the caller checks shared state again.

mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.title: Example: a bounded queue
mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.body: The consumer locks the queue and waits in a loop while it is empty. The producer inserts an item under the same lock and signals availability. The consumer rechecks because another consumer may win the item or the wake-up may be spurious. A signal sent before a waiter exists is harmless only if the actual predicate, such as a nonempty queue, remains recorded in shared state.

how-blocking-works.title: The lost-wake-up problem
how-blocking-works.body: A naive waiter checks that no work exists, then goes to sleep. If a producer publishes work and signals between those two actions, the waiter can sleep forever. Correct wait protocols couple condition checking with registration for notification. Linux futex-based designs combine an atomic user-space state with kernel-assisted waiting when the expected state still holds.

how-blocking-works.title: Example: uncontended and contended locking
how-blocking-works.body: On an uncontended fast path, an atomic update can acquire a mutex without a kernel wait. On contention, the implementation records waiting and parks through an appropriate kernel mechanism. Unlocking changes the state and may wake a waiter. Waking does not transfer CPU execution immediately and may not transfer ownership directly; the contender must follow the mutex's acquisition protocol.

spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.title: Spinning consumes the CPU while waiting
spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.body: A spinlock repeatedly checks for ownership instead of sleeping. It is suitable only when the expected wait is short and the holder can make progress. Interrupt and preemption constraints matter: an interrupt handler that spins on a lock held by the interrupted context on the same CPU can deadlock. Kernel lock variants encode these context-specific requirements.

spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.title: Example: choosing the wrong wait
spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.body: If a critical section performs disk I/O, a spinning contender can waste a full CPU while storage takes milliseconds. A sleeping lock is usually appropriate in a context allowed to sleep. Conversely, a context that must not schedule cannot simply substitute a mutex. Keep critical sections short, document lock context, and reason about who can interrupt whom, not just how many threads exist.

deadlock.title: Four conditions form a cycle
deadlock.body: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, holding resources while requesting more, lack of forced resource reclamation, and a circular dependency. Prevention breaks one of these conditions; avoidance reasons about safe allocation; detection finds cycles or equivalent evidence after they form. A timeout can limit waiting but does not automatically undo partially completed work or restore the application's invariant.

deadlock.title: Worked lock-order example
deadlock.body: Thread A holds lock X and waits for Y; thread B holds Y and waits for X. Neither can reach its unlock. Requiring every path to acquire X before Y removes that particular cycle. Ordering must include callbacks and error paths too. If acquiring many resources dynamically, sort by a stable identity or use a protocol that releases and retries without leaving partial updates behind.

starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.title: Progress failures have different mechanisms
starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.body: Starvation means a task never receives the resource it needs while others progress. Livelock means tasks remain active but repeatedly undo or avoid each other without useful completion. Priority inversion means urgent work depends on a resource held by lower-priority work, potentially delayed by intermediate-priority tasks. Different mechanisms require different remedies; adding a timeout does not identify the cause.

starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.title: Example: inversion across three tasks
starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.body: Low-priority L holds a mutex. High-priority H blocks on it. Medium-priority M remains runnable and prevents L from finishing, indirectly delaying H. Priority inheritance temporarily raises the relevant holder's priority so it can release the lock. It does not eliminate long critical sections or arbitrary dependency chains. For livelock in symmetric retries, randomized backoff may help where priority inheritance cannot.

pipes-and-fifos.title: A byte stream with endpoint lifetimes
pipes-and-fifos.body: A pipe carries bytes between a read end and a write end. Reads do not necessarily correspond one-to-one with writes, so applications still need framing. A FIFO adds a filesystem name for connecting processes. Kernel buffering has finite capacity: a writer can block or receive a would-block result when consumers do not drain data quickly enough.

pipes-and-fifos.title: Example: a pipeline that never finishes
pipes-and-fifos.body: A parent creates a pipe, launches a writer and reader, but accidentally keeps its own write descriptor open. After the writer exits, the reader can still wait because at least one write end remains open. Close unused ends in every process. Small writes may have atomicity guarantees up to a platform limit, but arbitrary large messages are not atomic records.

shared-memory.title: Shared bytes need a protocol
shared-memory.body: Mapping the same storage into several processes avoids copying every message through a stream API. It does not provide ownership, message boundaries, ordering, or crash recovery by itself. Use synchronization intended for inter-process use and define when a record becomes valid. Pointers stored inside a shared region may be meaningless at another mapping address; offsets are often safer.

shared-memory.title: Example: publishing a ring-buffer slot
shared-memory.body: A producer reserves a slot, writes its payload, then publishes completion with the required memory ordering. A consumer must not read merely because the index was allocated. After consumption, ownership returns to the producer. Generation information distinguishes reused slots. Specify what happens if a producer dies after reserving a slot but before publishing it, so readers do not wait forever.

message-queues-and-signals.title: Records versus notifications
message-queues-and-signals.body: A message queue preserves message-oriented structure and may offer ordering, priorities, and bounded capacity. Signals primarily notify; ordinary signals are not a durable arbitrary-length message stream. Choose based on payload needs, backpressure, and delivery semantics. Even a queue does not guarantee that a recipient completed the requested operation merely because the send succeeded.

message-queues-and-signals.title: Example: worker dispatch
message-queues-and-signals.body: A dispatcher sends a job identifier and the worker acknowledges completion separately. If the worker dies after processing but before acknowledging, a retry can duplicate effects, so the operation needs deduplication or idempotency. Bound the queue and define producer behavior when it fills. Signals can announce available work if the actual jobs remain safely recorded elsewhere.

unix-domain-sockets.title: Local communication with socket semantics
unix-domain-sockets.body: Unix domain sockets connect processes on one host and provide stream or message-oriented behavior depending on type. They avoid IP routing while retaining familiar send, receive, and readiness patterns. Some platforms support passing descriptor references and checking peer credentials. A filesystem pathname is one naming option; permissions, collisions, and cleanup require deliberate handling.

unix-domain-sockets.title: Example: passing an open resource
unix-domain-sockets.body: A supervisor opens a file under controlled authority and passes a descriptor through the supported ancillary-data mechanism. The worker receives a usable reference, not merely the sender's integer descriptor number. Define who closes each reference and whether access should survive a privilege change. Passing a descriptor transfers capability to an already opened object and deserves explicit ownership rules.

network-sockets-and-the-kernel.title: Several queues lie behind accept
network-sockets-and-the-kernel.body: A listening socket has connection-establishment state and a queue of connections available for acceptance; accepted sockets have their own send and receive buffers. Backlog settings constrain parts of this path but do not create unlimited workers or throughput. A successful accept returns a new descriptor for one connection rather than replacing the listening socket.

network-sockets-and-the-kernel.title: Example: fast handshakes, slow requests
network-sockets-and-the-kernel.body: A server accepts connections faster than workers can read them. Accepted sockets accumulate and consume descriptors and buffers; clients experience application timeouts despite successful handshakes. Increasing the listen backlog addresses waiting before acceptance only. Bound admitted connections and work, monitor queue stages separately, and close abandoned connections so added capacity does not simply relocate the bottleneck.

zero-copy-transfers.title: Avoiding copies does not remove ownership
zero-copy-transfers.body: Ordinary forwarding can copy bytes from a kernel buffer into user memory and back into another kernel buffer. Interfaces such as sendfile and splice avoid some copies on supported paths. mmap provides address-space access to backing storage but still involves faults, caches, and synchronization. Zero-copy describes a particular data path, not a universal guarantee about an operation.

zero-copy-transfers.title: Example: serving a large file
zero-copy-transfers.body: A server transfers a static file to a socket and loops until the requested range is sent. Partial progress and would-block results still need handling. Transformations or encryption may change the path and savings. Keep source contents stable for the required lifetime and measure CPU, memory bandwidth, and throughput rather than assuming the API name proves the benefit.

the-io-path.title: Acceptance and completion differ
the-io-path.body: A buffered write commonly copies bytes into cached pages, marks them dirty, and returns before storage persists them. Later write-back constructs device requests; the controller and medium complete them according to their guarantees. File metadata, allocation, and ordering add work around the payload. Device completion must be interpreted together with device caches and flush semantics.

the-io-path.title: Example: a log during a crash
the-io-path.body: An application prints a log line but crashes before flushing its user-space buffer; the kernel may never receive it. After a successful write, bytes may reach the page cache but remain vulnerable to power loss. Durability requires appropriate synchronization and error checks. Trace language buffers, kernel caches, device queues, and persistent media separately instead of treating them as one boundary.

device-controllers-interrupts-and-dma.title: Moving data without copying every byte on the CPU
device-controllers-interrupts-and-dma.body: A driver configures device operations. DMA lets a device transfer data into or out of suitable memory, while interrupts or polling report completion. Buffers must remain valid during transfer, and device-visible addresses need appropriate mapping and synchronization. An IOMMU can restrict and translate device access rather than granting devices unrestricted reach into physical memory.

device-controllers-interrupts-and-dma.title: Example: receiving a packet
device-controllers-interrupts-and-dma.body: A driver prepares buffers and descriptors. The device places incoming bytes into a buffer and reports completion. The driver or deferred processing path validates metadata and hands data onward, then replenishes buffers. If buffers are exhausted, traffic may drop even while application CPUs are idle. Device completion does not mean the application has consumed the packet or finished processing its request.

blocking-and-non-blocking-io.title: When progress is unavailable
blocking-and-non-blocking-io.body: A blocking operation may suspend the caller until it can make progress or report an error. A nonblocking operation returns promptly when it cannot proceed, often with EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK on Unix sockets. Prompt return does not guarantee transferring the full requested buffer. Regular files and special devices can have different behavior from network sockets.

blocking-and-non-blocking-io.title: Example: sending a response
blocking-and-non-blocking-io.body: A nonblocking send accepts 300 bytes of a 1,000-byte response. Retain the remaining 700 bytes and their offset. Wait for readiness rather than spinning continuously. Retry and handle partial progress again. If the peer closes, report or discard unfinished work according to the protocol; the earlier partial success is not proof the complete response reached the remote application.

synchronous-and-asynchronous-io.title: Waiting and completion are separate axes
synchronous-and-asynchronous-io.body: A synchronous API reports the operation's result through the call performing it, even if its nonblocking variant reports would-block. An asynchronous API separates submission from completion through events, callbacks, futures, or completion queues. A runtime may implement its asynchronous interface using worker threads rather than device-level async operations. The interface does not by itself reveal the implementation.

synchronous-and-asynchronous-io.title: Example: buffer lifetime
synchronous-and-asynchronous-io.body: After submitting an asynchronous write, do not overwrite or free the source buffer until the contract permits it. Submission success means the request entered a processing path; completion can still report failure or partial transfer. Associate request identifiers with buffers so out-of-order completions update the correct operation. Cancellation can race with completion and must have a defined cleanup path.

io-multiplexing.title: One waiter can serve many descriptors
io-multiplexing.body: select, poll, and epoll let an execution context wait for activity across descriptors. select uses descriptor sets with platform-specific limits; poll uses an array; epoll maintains an interest set. Costs depend on descriptor count, active fraction, and registration churn. None parses application messages or guarantees that one event corresponds to one complete request.

io-multiplexing.title: Example: a thousand idle clients
io-multiplexing.body: A server registers client sockets and sleeps until some can progress. When ten become readable, it processes bounded work from those ten. Connections can close while events remain pending, so descriptor reuse and object lifetime need careful handling. Keep application connection identity separate from a numeric descriptor that the OS can later assign to a different connection.

readiness-and-completion-models.title: An invitation versus a result
readiness-and-completion-models.body: Readiness says an operation is likely able to progress now, but another actor can change the state before the call. Completion says a submitted operation produced a result. Level-triggered readiness remains reportable while its condition holds. Edge-triggered notification reports transitions and requires consumers to drain or otherwise track pending work before waiting for another transition.

readiness-and-completion-models.title: Example: an edge-triggered stall
readiness-and-completion-models.body: A socket contains three messages, but the handler reads one and waits again. If it remains readable and no new edge occurs, the remaining messages can stall. Nonblocking handlers commonly read until would-block while preserving fairness for other clients. Re-arming and one-shot modes impose additional duties; follow the actual API contract rather than applying one event-loop recipe everywhere.

io-uring.title: Submission and completion rings
io-uring.body: io_uring provides queues for describing operations and receiving results. Applications associate identifiers with work and interpret completions independently of submission order. Some operations finish immediately; others wait or use worker paths. Shared rings reduce certain boundary overheads, but supported operations, restrictions, and advantages depend on the kernel, configuration, and workload. They do not eliminate error handling.

io-uring.title: Example: several reads in flight
io-uring.body: Submit reads for blocks A, B, and C with distinct identifiers. If B completes first, place its result in B's destination rather than assuming submission order. Maintain buffer ownership until completion and inspect every result. Queue saturation, cancellation, and failure of linked operations require explicit handling: successful submission does not mean every requested read completed successfully.

event-loops-reactor-and-proactor.title: Where the work happens
event-loops-reactor-and-proactor.body: A reactor waits for readiness and then performs nonblocking operations. A proactor submits operations and reacts to completion. An event loop coordinates the model exposed by its platform and runtime. Callbacks should do bounded work so one connection cannot monopolize dispatch. Timers, cancellation, and application queues also consume the event loop's limited processing capacity.

event-loops-reactor-and-proactor.title: Example: blocking in a callback
event-loops-reactor-and-proactor.body: An event loop handles socket readiness quickly but makes a synchronous database call inside one callback. Unrelated connections on that loop now wait behind the database. A bounded executor or appropriate async database interface restores overlap, but an unlimited offload queue merely relocates the problem. Carry request deadlines and cancellation across the boundary so abandoned work does not accumulate.

buffering-and-backpressure.title: Buffers absorb bursts, not sustained overload
buffering-and-backpressure.body: When arrivals exceed service, queued work grows until capacity runs out. Backpressure communicates reduced capacity upstream or stops accepting more work. A buffer trades memory and waiting time for burst tolerance. Define whether a full queue blocks, rejects, drops, or coalesces work based on the data's semantics and whether its producer can actually slow down.

buffering-and-backpressure.title: Worked capacity example
buffering-and-backpressure.body: A producer creates 120 items per second and a consumer handles 100. An empty 200-item buffer fills in 200/(120−100)=10 seconds in a constant-rate model. Doubling it delays failure to 20 seconds but does not repair the mismatch. Reduce input, increase sustainable service, or discard permissible work. Monitor queue age as well as length because a modest queue can still contain expired requests.

event-driven-servers-in-production.title: Connection state is explicit
event-driven-servers-in-production.body: A production server tracks partial reads, parsing state, pending writes, deadlines, and closure for each connection. Event-driven does not mean stateless. Limit memory per connection and work per event, and protect the event loop from blocking calls. Shutdown must account for registered events and in-flight operations before destroying connection objects or reusing their identifiers.

event-driven-servers-in-production.title: Example: a slow reader
event-driven-servers-in-production.body: A client sends a small request but consumes its response one byte at a time. Unlimited response production can hold large buffers indefinitely. Pause production when pending output reaches a bound, impose a progress deadline, and close according to policy if progress stays insufficient. Fair dispatch prevents that connection from consuming the service budget needed by other clients.

the-process-address-space.title: Regions have purposes and permissions
the-process-address-space.body: An address space contains mappings for code, static data, heap allocations, stacks, shared libraries, and other objects. Layout varies with architecture and randomization. A reserved virtual range is not necessarily backed by resident frames. Read, write, and execute permissions protect mappings independently of whether a pointer's numeric value looks plausible or lies near a valid object.

the-process-address-space.title: Example: a large reservation
the-process-address-space.body: Reserve a large anonymous range and touch only one page. Virtual size can rise substantially while resident memory grows much less. Touching every page changes physical demand and may expose limits that reservation did not. Track residency and application ownership separately; successful reservation does not prove every future access can be serviced cheaply or that memory pressure cannot later interrupt progress.

logical-and-physical-memory.title: Translation preserves a useful illusion
logical-and-physical-memory.body: Programs use virtual addresses interpreted through the active translation context. Physical addresses identify memory-system locations. Two processes can use the same virtual address for different frames, and two virtual addresses can map one frame. Paging translates the page number while preserving the within-page offset. Permissions are checked along with translation rather than inferred from the resulting address alone.

logical-and-physical-memory.title: Worked address translation
logical-and-physical-memory.body: With a 4,096-byte page, virtual address 0x3123 has page number 3 and offset 0x123. If page 3 maps to frame 9, the physical address is 0x9123. Missing mappings and prohibited accesses cannot be repaired with arithmetic; they enter a fault path. Changing a mapping also requires appropriate handling of translations cached by CPUs using that address space.

contiguous-allocation-and-fragmentation.title: Free space can be unusable
contiguous-allocation-and-fragmentation.body: External fragmentation splits free space into holes too small for a contiguous request. Internal fragmentation wastes capacity inside allocated units. First-fit and best-fit policies trade search work against future hole patterns. Compaction requires moving allocations safely, which is not always possible for pinned or externally exposed addresses. Total free capacity therefore does not determine the largest satisfiable allocation.

contiguous-allocation-and-fragmentation.title: Example: enough total, insufficient contiguous space
contiguous-allocation-and-fragmentation.body: Free holes of 3, 4, and 5 units total 12, but none satisfies an 8-unit contiguous allocation. Coalescing helps only when holes are adjacent in the relevant allocator. Paging reduces applications' need for physically contiguous storage, but devices, huge pages, and low-level allocators may still require it. Distinguish physical contiguity from a continuous range of virtual addresses.

segmentation.title: Named regions with bounds
segmentation.body: Segmentation represents regions such as code, data, and stack through a base and limit in a simple model. An offset is checked against bounds and translated using the base. This expresses protection and sharing at region granularity, but variable-size regions introduce fragmentation and growth problems. Hardware implementations differ, so the educational model must not be mistaken for every modern CPU's active translation mode.

segmentation.title: Worked bounds check
segmentation.body: A segment begins at physical address 20,000 and has length 4,000. Offset 1,500 maps to 21,500; offset 4,000 is outside the zero-based region. Paging instead divides regions into fixed-size units, allowing noncontiguous frames. Compare which metadata is needed and where wasted space occurs in each model before deciding that one is simply a larger or smaller version of the other.

how-malloc-works.title: The allocator sits above virtual memory
how-malloc-works.body: malloc manages user-space metadata and often obtains larger regions from the OS before subdividing them. Freed blocks may stay in arenas for reuse rather than returning immediately to the kernel. Size classes, alignment, thread caches, and fragmentation make requested bytes differ from resident memory. free ends the caller's ownership; it does not promise zeroed storage or a lower RSS.

how-malloc-works.title: Example: many small objects
how-malloc-works.body: A million 24-byte objects can consume more than 24 million bytes because of rounding, metadata, page layout, and retained free space. An object pool may improve locality and reduce overhead but introduces more lifetime management. Profile allocation sites and retained objects before blaming the kernel. Also distinguish memory retained for reuse from memory still reachable through a genuine application leak.

kernel-memory-allocation.title: Allocation contexts constrain recovery
kernel-memory-allocation.body: Kernel allocators manage physical pages and smaller objects. Buddy-style allocation tracks power-of-two page blocks; slab-style allocators reuse storage for common object types. An allocation also has context constraints: may it sleep, reclaim memory, or perform I/O? Interrupt-sensitive or atomic contexts cannot assume the same recovery paths as ordinary process-context code, even for identical allocation sizes.

kernel-memory-allocation.title: Example: failure despite free pages
kernel-memory-allocation.body: A driver requests a large physically contiguous block. Many free pages exist, but no suitable run is available, so allocation fails. Repeatedly retrying in a context that cannot reclaim safely is not a solution. Use the interface designed for the device and lifetime, and establish whether it needs physical contiguity, virtual contiguity, or scatter-gather support before selecting an allocator.

memory-metrics.title: Each number answers a different question
memory-metrics.body: Virtual size measures mappings. RSS measures resident pages attributed to a process, including shared pages. PSS apportions shared pages among their sharers. None equals the current size of application objects. Allocator retention, libraries, file-backed pages, and kernel memory complicate diagnosis. Explain the accounting boundary and sampling interval before comparing two process sizes or adding measurements across a fleet.

memory-metrics.title: Worked sharing example
memory-metrics.body: Two processes each use 10 MiB privately and share 20 MiB. Each may show about 30 MiB RSS, giving a misleading 60 MiB sum even though the combined pages occupy 40 MiB. Under equal sharing, each PSS is roughly 20 MiB. Additional kernel allocations and reporting details can change actual figures; use this example to understand attribution rather than as a complete host-memory formula.

memory-pressure-and-the-oom-killer.title: Pressure has costs before failure
memory-pressure-and-the-oom-killer.body: The kernel can reclaim clean cached pages, write dirty pages, or swap eligible anonymous pages when configured. Reclaim and repeated faults add latency long before an allocation fails. When constraints cannot be satisfied, an out-of-memory action may terminate a task. A container limit can cause local pressure while the host still has unused memory, so host totals alone are insufficient.

memory-pressure-and-the-oom-killer.title: Example: a cache becomes harmful
memory-pressure-and-the-oom-killer.body: An application enlarges its cache until useful filesystem pages are repeatedly reclaimed. Its own cache hit rate improves while storage traffic and tail latency worsen. Size it against the total working set, not its isolated hit rate. Examine cgroup events, resident trends, swap activity, and completed requests to distinguish a leak, temporary demand, and a workload that permanently exceeds its budget.

why-virtual-memory-exists.title: Isolation and flexible placement
why-virtual-memory-exists.body: Virtual memory gives a process a consistent address-space abstraction while physical pages can be placed, shared, protected, or populated on demand. It supports mapped files and copy-on-write. It does not create infinite capacity: page tables, resident frames, backing storage, and fault handling consume resources. The benefit is flexible management with controlled access, not eliminating physical limits.

why-virtual-memory-exists.title: Example: independent layouts
why-virtual-memory-exists.body: Two applications can place data at virtual address 0x400000 while the kernel maps them to different frames. Read-only library pages may instead reference common frames. These decisions happen below ordinary pointer arithmetic. A bad pointer is judged against the current mappings and permissions, not against whether another process happens to use the same numeric address successfully.

the-mmu-and-address-translation.title: Hardware enforces the active mapping
the-mmu-and-address-translation.body: The MMU translates addresses and checks permissions through mapping structures and cached entries. A translation-cache miss requires finding the mapping through the architecture's page-table mechanism. A valid translation does not imply a valid operation: writing a read-only resident page can fault even when its frame is known. Separate finding the address from authorizing the access.

the-mmu-and-address-translation.title: Example: changing permissions
the-mmu-and-address-translation.body: Removing write access updates mapping metadata, but a CPU might still hold an older translation. The OS performs the required invalidation and synchronization, sometimes across several CPUs using the address space. Mapping changes can therefore cost more than updating a table entry. Correctness requires that stale writable translations cannot survive beyond the operation's promised protection boundary.

paging.title: Fixed units separate allocation from placement
paging.body: Paging divides virtual ranges into pages and physical memory into frames. Page-table entries connect them and carry information such as permissions and residency. A large virtual range no longer needs one continuous physical allocation. The costs include metadata, translation work, and unused capacity in partly occupied pages. Page size affects all three trade-offs rather than only the number of entries.

paging.title: Worked page count
paging.body: A 10,000-byte range starting at a page boundary touches three 4,096-byte pages. Their combined capacity is 12,288 bytes, leaving 2,288 beyond the requested length in the last page. This describes mapped capacity, not necessarily resident frames. An unaligned start can touch another boundary. Work out both start offset and length before estimating page count for an arbitrary buffer.

multilevel-page-tables.title: Sparse spaces need sparse metadata
multilevel-page-tables.body: A flat table for every possible virtual page would waste memory in sparse address spaces. Multilevel tables allocate lower levels only where needed. Address bits index successive levels and the final offset chooses a byte. More levels save unused metadata but can add memory accesses on translation misses; caches and supported large-page entries reduce some of that work.

multilevel-page-tables.title: Worked scale estimate
multilevel-page-tables.body: A 4 KiB table with 8-byte entries holds 512 entries. A leaf describing 4 KiB pages covers 2 MiB. Higher levels reference more tables rather than requiring every leaf to exist in advance. Large-page entries can terminate the walk earlier on supported hardware, but exchange fine-grained mapping flexibility for larger allocation and protection units. The exact level count is architecture-dependent.

the-tlb.title: Translations are cached separately from data
the-tlb.body: The TLB stores mappings and permissions so most memory operations avoid page-table walks. A miss can resolve from an existing valid mapping without a page fault or disk access. Context identifiers may allow entries from different address spaces to coexist. Invalidation is required when mappings or permissions change, and its scope depends on the architecture and operation.

the-tlb.title: Example: translation reach
the-tlb.body: A simplified 64-entry TLB mapping 4 KiB pages covers 256 KiB at once. Random accesses across thousands of pages can exceed that reach even with every page resident. Larger pages increase reach but have other costs. Associativity, separate instruction/data structures, and additional translation-cache levels mean this capacity calculation is a starting model, not a prediction of every actual miss.

page-faults.title: Classify the cause and legal recovery
page-faults.body: A fault may mean a valid page needs population, a copy-on-write transition is required, or the access is invalid. The handler checks mapping and operation before deciding whether recovery is legal. Minor faults generally avoid storage I/O; major faults require it under the relevant accounting model. A recoverable fault can still be slow enough to affect application deadlines.

page-faults.title: Example: three writes, different outcomes
page-faults.body: Writing a newly mapped anonymous page may allocate a zero-filled frame. Writing a private copy-on-write page may allocate and copy a frame. Writing an unmapped address should fail rather than grant arbitrary memory. Successful recovery lets the instruction resume. Compare fault counts with access patterns and I/O instead of combining all faults into one supposed measure of errors or disk activity.

demand-paging.title: Populate when access creates demand
demand-paging.body: Demand paging postpones materializing a page until it is touched. This reduces startup and residency for unused code and data but moves work onto first access. Read-ahead and prefetching can anticipate later accesses. Reserving an address, reading it, and writing it may therefore have distinct physical consequences. A mapping operation alone does not reveal steady-state memory demand.

demand-paging.title: Example: the cold first request
demand-paging.body: A service maps a model at startup but touches only metadata. Its first request accesses many new pages and pays fault and possibly storage costs. Warming representative pages improves predictability at the cost of startup time and memory pressure. Measure cold and warm requests separately and warm only what the intended memory budget can keep resident without displacing other useful work.

page-replacement-algorithms.title: Choose a victim under capacity pressure
page-replacement-algorithms.body: FIFO evicts the earliest-loaded page; LRU favors recently used pages; clock-style policies approximate recency using reference information. The offline optimal policy knows future accesses and is a comparison baseline, not a practical predictor. Dirty victims may need write-back, so eviction cost and future usefulness both matter. Perfect LRU bookkeeping also has costs that simplified exercises omit.

page-replacement-algorithms.title: Worked reference sequence
page-replacement-algorithms.body: With three empty frames and references 1,2,3,1,4, FIFO evicts 1 on the final reference because it arrived first. LRU evicts 2 because 1 was recently used. A subsequent reference to 1 faults under FIFO and hits under LRU. Compare other patterns before declaring a universal winner; FIFO can even experience more faults with additional frames on certain reference sequences.

working-sets-and-thrashing.title: The active set determines sustainable residency
working-sets-and-thrashing.body: A working set is the collection of pages needed during a relevant recent interval. If competing active sets exceed usable memory, pages can be evicted just before reuse. Increasing time goes into reclaim and faults rather than useful work. High storage activity with low useful CPU throughput can therefore originate in memory pressure instead of slow application computation.

working-sets-and-thrashing.title: Example: too many large workers
working-sets-and-thrashing.body: A worker scans a 300 MiB active set repeatedly. Eight such workers cannot keep their active data resident in 1 GiB available to them. Reducing concurrency can improve throughput by avoiding repeated eviction. Compare fault rates, reclaim pressure, and completions together. More workers do not necessarily create more effective capacity when their aggregate working sets overwhelm the memory hierarchy.

copy-on-write.title: Share first, separate on mutation
copy-on-write.body: Copy-on-write lets independent logical owners initially reference common contents. Relevant mappings prevent uncontrolled writes. A write fault prompts the OS to determine whether private backing is needed, arrange it, update translation, and resume. The optimization postpones copying; it does not remove later memory demand or guarantee that every fault must copy if the page has become exclusively owned.

copy-on-write.title: Example: a snapshotting process
copy-on-write.body: A parent with a large heap starts a child snapshot. Initially many pages remain shared, but subsequent writes create private versions. Memory can rise sharply without a matching new malloc call. Budget for the pages dirtied during the snapshot interval rather than only the child's initial RSS. Long snapshots allow more divergence and can therefore have a larger transient memory cost.

mmap-and-memory-mapped-files.title: Mapping mode defines write behavior
mmap-and-memory-mapped-files.body: A file mapping connects a file range to virtual addresses.
