Shared mappings can expose changes through common backing; private mappings provide private modifications. Access still involves permissions, faults, and file-lifetime issues. Closing the descriptor does not by itself remove a successful mapping. Unmapping controls that mapping's lifetime, and persistence requires following the appropriate synchronization contract.

mmap-and-memory-mapped-files.title: Example: a changing backing file
mmap-and-memory-mapped-files.body: A reader maps a file while another actor later truncates it. Addresses within the old mapped range may now fault rather than return an ordinary read error. Coordinate mutation or replacement and bound access to the intended object. Mapped writes are not automatically atomic persistent transactions; design consistency, synchronization, and recovery separately from the convenience of pointer-based access.

shared-libraries-and-shared-pages.title: Code sharing does not share all state
shared-libraries-and-shared-pages.body: Read-only library instructions can use common physical pages across processes, while writable state is usually private unless explicitly shared. Relocations and loader behavior influence what stays shareable. Position-independent code helps avoid private instruction modifications when libraries load at different addresses. Shared physical storage does not require identical virtual addresses in every process using the library.

shared-libraries-and-shared-pages.title: Example: estimating many instances
shared-libraries-and-shared-pages.body: Ten processes load one library. Adding resident mappings can count common code ten times, although its physical pages exist once. The library's writable caches may still be private and multiply with instance count. Separate read-only sharing from mutable growth, and use proportional attribution where useful, before claiming that a library adds its full on-disk size to every process's physical footprint.

huge-pages-numa-and-aslr.title: Three mechanisms, different purposes
huge-pages-numa-and-aslr.body: Huge pages reduce translation entries but increase allocation granularity and potential waste. NUMA changes memory-access cost according to placement relative to the CPU. ASLR randomizes virtual layout to hinder some exploitation techniques. These mechanisms do not substitute for one another: randomization does not create locality, and larger pages do not enforce object-level bounds or correct unsafe application pointers.

huge-pages-numa-and-aslr.title: Example: moving away from memory
huge-pages-numa-and-aslr.body: A worker initializes an array on one NUMA node and later executes mainly on another. Remote access can reduce performance despite apparently sufficient aggregate CPU and RAM. Placement policy, first-touch behavior, and migration matter. Evaluate huge pages separately under the actual pattern, and keep security decisions distinct from performance tuning rather than disabling address randomization as a default remedy.

the-file-abstraction.title: Names, objects, and open references
the-file-abstraction.body: A file presents a byte-oriented object with metadata and operations, hiding physical block placement. Its pathname is a way to find it, not its identity for every purpose. Opening creates a reference used by later operations. Renaming or unlinking a name can therefore have different effects from closing an open reference, and behavior varies with platform contracts.

the-file-abstraction.title: Example: rotating a log
the-file-abstraction.body: A process keeps writing through an open descriptor while another process renames the log and creates a new file at the old pathname. On Unix the existing descriptor can keep referring to the original object. The writer must deliberately reopen or participate in rotation. Looking only at the current pathname can make apparently missing log output or retained disk usage confusing.

file-descriptors.title: An integer indexes a reference table
file-descriptors.body: A descriptor is local to a process's descriptor table and refers to an open object. The open file description holds state such as the current offset and relevant flags. Duplicated descriptors can reference the same description, while independent opens can have independent offsets. Descriptor numbers can be reused after close, so they are not permanent object identities.

file-descriptors.title: Example: shared offset versus separate opens
file-descriptors.body: Duplicate a descriptor and read 10 bytes through the first. A read through the duplicate can continue at the shared offset rather than restarting. Opening the same pathname twice generally creates independent open descriptions. Choose positional I/O when independent offsets are required, and track descriptor lifetime carefully so an old asynchronous callback cannot act on a newly reused integer.

file-operations.title: Successful calls can make partial progress
file-operations.body: Open, read, write, seek, close, and synchronization operations have distinct contracts. A write may transfer fewer bytes than requested; a read may return less without reaching end-of-file. Retrying must preserve completed progress. Seeking changes an offset on suitable objects but does not make sense for every stream, such as a pipe or ordinary network socket.

file-operations.title: Example: copying a file correctly
file-operations.body: Read into a bounded buffer, then keep writing from the unconsumed offset until all bytes from that read are handled. Check every return value and distinguish interruption from permanent errors. Stop on end-of-file and report relevant write or close failures. A loop assuming each write consumes the entire buffer can silently lose data under conditions absent from a small local test.

directories-and-path-resolution.title: Resolution traverses names and boundaries
directories-and-path-resolution.body: A directory maps names to filesystem objects. Resolving a pathname walks components relative to a root or current directory and may cross mounts or follow symbolic links. Permissions must permit traversal, not merely access to the final file. Concurrent renames and symlink changes can make a pathname identify a different object between two separate operations.

directories-and-path-resolution.title: Example: check-then-open is racy
directories-and-path-resolution.body: An application checks that a pathname looks safe and then opens it. Another actor changes a component between those operations, so the open reaches something else. Use directory-relative APIs and appropriate resolution restrictions where available, keeping trusted directory references rather than repeatedly resolving a mutable path. Validate the opened object when the security decision depends on its actual identity.

inodes.title: Metadata and names are separate
inodes.body: In inode-based filesystems, an inode represents metadata and references to file contents, while directory entries associate names with that inode. An inode number is meaningful within its filesystem and can be reused after deletion. The inode does not generally store every pathname pointing to it. Hard-link count and open references govern different aspects of lifetime.

inodes.title: Example: deleting one of two names
inodes.body: Names report.txt and backup.txt can be hard links to one inode. Removing report.txt removes one directory entry and decreases the link count without deleting backup.txt's contents. If all names disappear but a process retains an open reference, storage can remain until that reference closes. This explains why deleting a large open file may not immediately free its occupied space.

hard-and-symbolic-links.title: Object reference versus path text
hard-and-symbolic-links.body: A hard link adds another name for the same filesystem object, normally within the same filesystem. A symbolic link stores a pathname resolved when followed; it can cross filesystem boundaries and can become dangling. Renaming the target affects these mechanisms differently. Treating them as identical shortcuts leads to incorrect assumptions about deletion, permissions, and deployment updates.

hard-and-symbolic-links.title: Example: replacing a release
hard-and-symbolic-links.body: A stable symlink points to releases/v1. Updating it to releases/v2 redirects future path resolution, while already open files can remain associated with v1. A hard link to a file in v1 still names that original object even if another file appears at the old target pathname. Coordinate active readers and cleanup; changing a link does not instantly replace all existing open references.

file-permissions.title: Directory permissions have special meanings
file-permissions.body: For ordinary files, read and write control access to contents while execute permits execution subject to other checks. For directories, read concerns listing names, execute permits traversal, and write permits modifying entries with other constraints. Ownership, groups, ACLs, mount options, and security modules can all affect the final decision. A single mode-bit display may not explain every denial.

file-permissions.title: Example: deleting a read-only file
file-permissions.body: A user may be unable to write a file's contents yet still remove its directory entry when the containing directory permits that operation. Conversely, having permission to read the file does not guarantee permission to traverse every directory leading to it. Diagnose the requested operation and each relevant object; do not assume a file's write bit alone controls deletion.

the-vfs-layer.title: One interface, many implementations
the-vfs-layer.body: The virtual filesystem layer presents common operations while filesystem-specific code implements storage and naming behavior. An open reference can dispatch through operations suited to its underlying object. Uniform API names do not make every filesystem's durability, locking, or metadata semantics identical. Network-backed filesystems introduce additional failure and consistency boundaries behind familiar operations.

the-vfs-layer.title: Example: local versus remote storage
the-vfs-layer.body: The same application read can be satisfied from a local cache or require a remote server response. A remote interruption can add errors and retries absent from an in-memory filesystem test. Verify required rename, locking, and synchronization guarantees on the actual deployment filesystem instead of treating successful compilation against the same file API as proof of identical behavior.

file-allocation-and-extents.title: Representing where file bytes live
file-allocation-and-extents.body: Allocation strategies map logical file offsets to storage blocks. Extents describe runs of contiguous blocks compactly, reducing metadata compared with listing every block individually. Fragmented growth needs more extents and may reduce sequential locality. Sparse files represent holes without allocating ordinary data blocks for every logical byte, so logical file length differs from actual allocated storage.

file-allocation-and-extents.title: Example: a sparse image
file-allocation-and-extents.body: Seek far beyond current end and write a small record on a filesystem supporting sparse behavior. The file's logical size becomes large, but the unwritten hole can read as zeros without consuming equivalent data blocks. Copying it through a tool that does not preserve holes may allocate much more storage. Compare logical size, allocated blocks, and filesystem capabilities before planning capacity.

dentry-and-inode-caches.title: Cache names and metadata as well as contents
dentry-and-inode-caches.body: The dentry cache accelerates name-to-object lookup; inode caches retain metadata-related objects. These differ from the page cache holding file data. A workload repeatedly opening tiny files can spend substantial work on name lookup and metadata even when payload bytes are small. Negative lookup caching can also remember that a name was absent, subject to invalidation rules.

dentry-and-inode-caches.title: Example: a directory-heavy workload
dentry-and-inode-caches.body: A build scans hundreds of thousands of paths while compiling little code. Warm runs may be faster because directory and inode information is cached, not merely because source contents are resident. Compare cold and warm metadata behavior and path counts. Avoid diagnosing every filesystem delay with sequential bandwidth tests, which exercise a different part of the storage stack.

crash-consistency.title: Multi-step updates can be interrupted
crash-consistency.body: Updating a file may require allocating blocks, changing data, updating metadata, and changing directory entries. A crash can interrupt these steps or expose persisted writes in an unexpected combination. Crash consistency defines which recoverable states are allowed. Application-level atomicity is stronger than merely avoiding structural filesystem corruption, so the filesystem and application each need an appropriate recovery design.

crash-consistency.title: Example: replacing configuration
crash-consistency.body: Write a complete new configuration to a temporary file in the target filesystem, synchronize it as required, rename it into place, and synchronize the containing directory when needed for the intended durability guarantee. Check errors at each stage. Rename can provide atomic namespace replacement under its contract, but atomic visibility and survival after power loss are separate properties.

journaling.title: Record recovery intent before final placement
journaling.body: A journal records information sufficient to recover selected updates after interruption. Metadata journaling protects filesystem structures; data journaling can cover payloads too, with different costs. Transaction boundaries, commit records, replay, and write ordering determine which operations are recovered. Journaling is not an automatic transaction system for several unrelated application files or a replacement for application synchronization.

journaling.title: Example: crash around a commit
journaling.body: If a journal transaction is incomplete, recovery must avoid applying a partial metadata change as committed work. If a valid commit exists but final locations were not updated, replay can finish the update. The exact guarantees depend on mode and filesystem. An application must still decide when to request durability and how to handle an error or ambiguous result.

copy-on-write-file-systems.title: Publish a new version through metadata
copy-on-write-file-systems.body: A copy-on-write filesystem writes new versions of modified blocks instead of overwriting the old version immediately, then updates metadata to reference a consistent new tree. Snapshots can retain old references efficiently. Shared blocks require reference tracking, and later modifications allocate additional space. Cheap snapshot creation does not mean snapshots are free to retain under ongoing writes.

copy-on-write-file-systems.title: Example: space retained by a snapshot
copy-on-write-file-systems.body: A large file is deleted from the active filesystem, but a snapshot still references its old blocks. Those blocks cannot be reclaimed just because the live pathname disappeared. Capacity planning must include retained versions and metadata. Write amplification, fragmentation, and checksumming behavior depend on implementation; compare actual workloads instead of equating all copy-on-write filesystems with one performance profile.

storage-hardware.title: Access patterns interact with the medium
storage-hardware.body: Hard disks pay mechanical seek and rotation costs, making sequential access especially valuable. SSDs eliminate mechanical motion but add flash translation, erase blocks, garbage collection, and endurance constraints. NVMe changes the interface and queueing model rather than making every operation equally fast. Device caches and power-loss protection affect persistence guarantees independently of headline throughput.

storage-hardware.title: Example: random small writes
storage-hardware.body: A workload issuing 4 KiB random writes stresses a different path from streaming large sequential buffers. An SSD may perform well initially and slow when internal maintenance or sustained-write limits become relevant. Test long enough to reach representative conditions, and distinguish device capability from filesystem overhead, queueing, and application durability requirements. One maximum bandwidth number cannot describe all these workloads.

storage-performance.title: Latency, IOPS, bandwidth, and queue depth
storage-performance.body: IOPS counts operations per second; bandwidth counts bytes per second; latency measures an operation's duration. Average request size connects the first two. Queue depth controls how much work is in flight and can improve utilization while increasing wait time. Read/write mix, locality, cache state, and durability mode must accompany measurements for comparisons to be meaningful.

storage-performance.title: Worked throughput estimate
storage-performance.body: At 10,000 operations per second with 4 KiB requests, payload throughput is about 39.1 MiB/s. The same IOPS with 64 KiB requests would imply much more bandwidth if the device and stack sustain it. Under steady-state assumptions, 2,000 IOPS with 5 ms average latency imply about ten operations in flight. Use consistent units and measure tail latency as well as averages.

disk-scheduling-algorithms.title: Reordering trades locality against waiting
disk-scheduling-algorithms.body: FCFS preserves arrival order; shortest-seek approaches favor nearby requests; SCAN-like policies move through address ranges in an organized direction. These ideas reduce mechanical movement but can disadvantage distant requests without fairness rules. SSDs change the trade-off because seek distance is no longer mechanical, yet queue management, deadlines, and fairness still matter at the block layer.

disk-scheduling-algorithms.title: Example: nearby requests keep arriving
disk-scheduling-algorithms.body: A disk continually receives requests near its current head position while an older request waits far away. Always choosing the nearest request can starve the distant one. A deadline or sweep policy limits that waiting at the cost of some locality. Specify the initial head position, direction, and arrival times before comparing seek totals in a scheduling exercise.

the-block-layer.title: Requests pass through several queues
the-block-layer.body: The block layer translates higher-level I/O into requests suitable for devices, potentially merging, splitting, scheduling, and distributing them among hardware queues. Device completion flows back toward waiting callers and cached state. Application operations do not map one-to-one to hardware requests: cache hits may issue none, while one large write may become several requests.

the-block-layer.title: Example: apparent request amplification
the-block-layer.body: An application issues a large write, but tracing shows multiple smaller block requests plus metadata activity. Alignment, filesystem allocation, device limits, and journaling can explain the difference. Correlate bytes and timing across layers rather than assuming each observed request represents a separate application write. Queueing at an upper layer can also make application latency much larger than device service time.

the-page-cache.title: Read reuse and deferred writes
the-page-cache.body: The page cache holds file-backed data in memory. Reads can reuse cached pages; buffered writes mark pages dirty for later write-back. Dirty-page limits prevent unlimited deferred work and can throttle writers. Clean cached pages are often reclaimable, but a large cache is not proof memory is wasted. Its value depends on reuse and competition with other working sets.

the-page-cache.title: Example: a fast write followed by a stall
the-page-cache.body: A burst of writes initially completes quickly into memory, making throughput look higher than the device's sustained rate. As dirty data accumulates, write-back and throttling expose the real bottleneck. Run a sufficiently long test and report synchronization behavior. Short benchmark results can describe cache absorption rather than sustainable persistent-storage performance.

buffered-and-direct-io.title: Bypassing a cache is a trade-off
buffered-and-direct-io.body: Buffered I/O benefits from the kernel page cache, read-ahead, and write aggregation. Direct I/O can bypass parts of that caching path under filesystem- and platform-specific alignment rules. It does not automatically guarantee durability or eliminate every cache. Applications choosing it often assume more responsibility for buffering, request sizing, and coordination with other access paths.

buffered-and-direct-io.title: Example: a database with its own cache
buffered-and-direct-io.body: A database may prefer direct I/O to avoid retaining the same data in both its buffer pool and the OS page cache. Poorly sized or misaligned requests can still fail or perform badly. Mixing buffered, mapped, and direct access to overlapping regions requires careful coherence reasoning. Benchmark the complete design rather than assuming less caching always means less overhead.

durability-and-fsync.title: Define which failure must be survived
durability-and-fsync.body: A successful write reports data accepted according to the API, not necessarily persistence through power loss. Synchronization requests push relevant updates toward durable storage and can report delayed errors. File contents and the directory entry naming the file are distinct durability concerns. Guarantees depend on the filesystem, device, and correctly honored flush semantics.

durability-and-fsync.title: Example: acknowledging a transaction
durability-and-fsync.body: If a service acknowledges a committed record before the necessary durability operation succeeds, a crash can lose an operation clients believe completed. Group commit amortizes synchronization across several records but introduces waiting for the group. Measure durability latency separately from buffered-write latency, and treat synchronization failures as meaningful failures rather than logging them while still returning success.

raid.title: Redundancy addresses some failures, not all
raid.body: Striping distributes blocks for capacity or performance; mirroring duplicates data; parity reconstructs missing blocks within the array's fault model. RAID 0 has no redundancy, RAID 1 mirrors, and common parity arrangements tolerate a bounded number of member failures. Rebuild work competes with application I/O, and correlated failures can exceed the assumed protection.

raid.title: Example: deletion is replicated too
raid.body: An application mistakenly deletes valuable data. A redundant array faithfully stores the deletion, so redundancy does not restore the lost version. Backups and tested recovery serve a different purpose. Also examine degraded-mode performance, rebuild duration, controller dependencies, and write-hole protection where relevant. Counting surviving disks alone does not prove the end-to-end durability of acknowledged application operations.

diagnosing-io-problems.title: Locate waiting before replacing hardware
diagnosing-io-problems.body: Measure application operation latency, queueing, filesystem behavior, and device activity over the same interval. Distinguish cache misses, durability waits, metadata work, and large transfer costs. Device utilization metrics require interpretation on parallel devices: a busy interval is not always a simple percentage of exhausted performance. Use request size and queue depth alongside latency.

diagnosing-io-problems.title: Example: high latency with modest bandwidth
diagnosing-io-problems.body: A service performs a durability operation after each tiny write. Total bytes per second stay low, but each request waits for a persistence round trip. A sequential bandwidth benchmark would miss this bottleneck. Batching may help if the application's acknowledgment contract permits it. Validate the new failure behavior before treating fewer sync calls as an unconditional improvement.

protection-vs-security.title: Mechanisms and threats are related but different
protection-vs-security.body: Protection controls which subjects can perform which operations on resources. Security evaluates whether those controls and surrounding processes resist threats such as impersonation, malicious input, and privilege escalation. Correct permission bits are useful but do not make a vulnerable privileged service safe. Begin with assets, trust boundaries, and attacker capabilities before choosing a defense.

protection-vs-security.title: Example: an authorized service with a bug
protection-vs-security.body: A service legitimately reads a private file but exposes its contents through an incorrectly authorized endpoint. Filesystem protection worked as configured; application authorization failed. Conversely a well-written endpoint cannot protect files that unrelated users can read directly. Trace authority through every layer and reduce privileges so a failure in one component has a smaller reachable damage set.

users-groups-and-permissions.title: Identity participates in access checks
users-groups-and-permissions.body: Processes carry credentials used by kernel authorization. Files have ownership and permission metadata, and groups provide a way to share selected access. Effective and real identities, supplementary groups, ACLs, and privilege transitions complicate the simple owner/group/other model. Inspect the credentials of the actual failing process instead of assuming they match the interactive shell that launched it.

users-groups-and-permissions.title: Example: a service cannot read configuration
users-groups-and-permissions.body: A configuration file is readable by the administrator but not the service account. Running the whole service as root hides the symptom while expanding its authority. Grant only the required access to the intended identity, including directory traversal. Recheck how credentials are established at startup and whether workers retain unnecessary privileges after opening required resources.

access-control-and-capabilities.title: Authority can be scoped to an operation
access-control-and-capabilities.body: Discretionary access control uses ownership and delegated permissions; mandatory policies impose additional constraints. Capability approaches represent authority to particular operations or objects. Linux capabilities split some traditional root powers, while an open descriptor can function as authority to an object. These concepts share least-privilege goals but are not interchangeable implementations of one universal mechanism.

access-control-and-capabilities.title: Example: bind once, then reduce authority
access-control-and-capabilities.body: A server may need limited startup authority to acquire a resource but not need it for ordinary request handling. Arrange startup to obtain what is required and then drop unnecessary authority using a correctly designed platform-specific mechanism. Verify inherited descriptors and child processes too. A privilege reduction that leaves powerful handles available may retain more effective access than expected.

memory-protection.title: Permissions protect pages, not every object
memory-protection.body: The OS uses mapping permissions and privilege checks to separate address spaces and restrict read, write, and execute access. Guard pages can catch certain boundary crossings; nonexecutable memory reduces some code-injection paths. These mechanisms do not prove a C pointer stays inside its allocation when neighboring objects share a writable page. Language-level memory safety addresses a finer-grained problem.

memory-protection.title: Example: executable data is not required
memory-protection.body: A program normally needs writable data and executable code, not arbitrary memory simultaneously writable and executable. Restricting those permissions reduces attack opportunities, but attackers may reuse existing instructions if memory corruption remains. Combine correct lifetimes and bounds, appropriate runtime mitigations, and minimal authority. A page fault catches some bad accesses, not every misuse that corrupts application state.

seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.title: Reduce the reachable kernel interface
seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.body: Seccomp can restrict which system calls a Linux process may make under a filter policy. It is useful when a worker needs a narrow operation set. It does not replace filesystem authorization, memory safety, or namespace isolation, and filtering call numbers alone may not express every desired object-level policy. Compatibility requires accounting for runtime and library behavior.

seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.title: Example: a parsing worker
seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.body: A worker receives input and returns a parsed result but should not create arbitrary new network connections. A policy can constrain unnecessary syscall paths after required initialization. Test both successful and exceptional inputs because logging, allocation, and runtime cleanup may use additional calls. Rejecting a syscall without a deliberate failure path can turn a security boundary into unexplained crashes or lost work.

resource-limits.title: Bound consumption as well as access
resource-limits.body: Resource limits constrain quantities such as descriptors, process counts, address space, or CPU time according to platform rules. Soft limits define the active threshold; hard limits bound permitted increases under the relevant privilege model. These limits are not identical to cgroup controls and do not all measure physical consumption. Applications must handle failure when reaching a configured limit.

resource-limits.title: Example: controlled descriptor exhaustion
resource-limits.body: A worker leaks one descriptor per request until open or accept fails. Raising its limit delays failure but does not repair ownership. Count descriptors by type and identify missing closes, including exception paths. Keep an operational reserve and define graceful overload behavior so the process can report errors and recover instead of failing every unrelated operation at once.

common-os-vulnerabilities.title: Boundary mistakes amplify authority
common-os-vulnerabilities.body: Memory corruption, unsafe path resolution, race conditions, and overly broad privileges can turn ordinary input into unauthorized behavior. A time-of-check/time-of-use bug arises when the checked fact changes before the protected operation. Integer overflow can turn a large requested size into a small allocation. Correctness must cover transitions and arithmetic, not merely validate an initial string.

common-os-vulnerabilities.title: Example: length multiplication
common-os-vulnerabilities.body: A request specifies count objects of size bytes. If count×size wraps before allocation, a small buffer may be allocated and later written as though it were large. Check arithmetic before multiplying and validate every derived length. Even with validation, retain least privilege so an unrelated memory bug does not grant unnecessary filesystem, network, or process-control authority.

side-channels.title: Observable behavior can reveal hidden state
side-channels.body: A side channel infers information from effects such as execution time, cache activity, or resource contention rather than reading protected data directly. Isolation of addresses does not eliminate shared microarchitectural state. Defenses depend on the threat: constant-time algorithms, reducing sharing, and platform mitigations address different paths. Avoid assuming all timing variation is a vulnerability or all isolation eliminates it.

side-channels.title: Example: secret-dependent comparison
side-channels.body: A comparison that returns at the first mismatching secret byte can expose differences correlated with matching prefixes. Repeated measurements may extract a signal despite noise. Use a vetted constant-time comparison for relevant secrets rather than improvising one, and consider the surrounding protocol too. Branch removal alone is not a complete proof because compiler transformations and memory access patterns also matter.

what-virtualization-is.title: Present a managed view of resources
what-virtualization-is.body: Virtualization interposes a layer between a consumer and physical resources so each consumer can operate against a controlled abstraction. CPU, memory, storage, and devices require different mechanisms. The abstraction enables isolation, consolidation, and migration but adds management and scheduling interactions. Distinguish a virtual resource's advertised capacity from the physical service available when several guests compete.

what-virtualization-is.title: Example: four busy guests
what-virtualization-is.body: Four virtual machines each see four virtual CPUs on a host with fewer physical execution slots than the aggregate demand. Every guest can report runnable work while the host must multiplex it. Increasing a guest's vCPU count does not create host capacity and may worsen scheduling interactions. Diagnose both guest demand and host contention before tuning the application scheduler.

virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.title: Guest kernels run under a managing layer
virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.body: A hypervisor controls guest execution and access to machine resources, using hardware support and device virtualization where available. Type-1 and type-2 labels describe broad deployment arrangements, but implementation details determine the actual path. Guests run their own kernels, which distinguishes a VM from a container sharing the host kernel. Device emulation and paravirtualized interfaces have different overheads.

virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.title: Example: two independent kernel environments
virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.body: Two guests can use different kernel versions and isolate many guest-kernel failures from one another, subject to hypervisor and hardware correctness. Their storage or network can still share a host bottleneck. A guest crash boundary is not a guarantee against common infrastructure failure. Track resource dependencies and recovery behavior outside the VM as well as inside it.

virtualized-memory.title: Two address mappings can be involved
virtualized-memory.body: A guest translates process virtual addresses to guest-physical addresses. The virtualization layer maps guest-physical memory to host backing, often with hardware-assisted nested translation. Translation caches reduce repeated work, but misses can involve extra lookup cost. Guest-visible free memory and host physical pressure are separate observations; overcommit and host reclaim can affect a guest unexpectedly.

virtualized-memory.title: Example: memory pressure at two levels
virtualized-memory.body: A guest believes it has enough memory, yet host contention delays access to its backing. Conversely the host may have spare RAM while a guest's internal allocation is constrained. Check both accounting layers before increasing an application heap. Huge pages, ballooning, and host allocation policies can influence performance, but their benefits depend on actual configuration and workload locality.

containers-vs-virtual-machines.title: Different kernel boundaries
containers-vs-virtual-machines.body: Containers isolate selected views and resource use for processes sharing a host kernel. Virtual machines run guest kernels behind a virtualization boundary. Containers often start quickly and package user space efficiently, but cannot supply arbitrary missing host-kernel behavior simply by installing different user-space files. VM isolation and container convenience can also be combined by running containers inside guests.

containers-vs-virtual-machines.title: Example: a kernel-specific feature
containers-vs-virtual-machines.body: A container image includes a tool expecting a newer syscall than the host supports. The executable can exist and its libraries can load, yet the call fails because the host kernel implements the interface. A VM with a suitable guest kernel addresses a different layer. Diagnose the missing contract rather than repeatedly rebuilding the image with the same kernel assumption.

namespaces.title: Isolate views of selected resources
namespaces.body: Linux namespaces provide separate views for resources such as process IDs, mounts, networking, and hostnames. User namespaces introduce identity mapping with specific privilege rules. Joining one namespace does not automatically isolate every resource or enforce consumption limits. The process still participates in a shared host kernel, and access through retained references can cross assumptions about visible names.

namespaces.title: Example: two processes called PID 1
namespaces.body: Two containers can each see a process numbered 1 in their PID namespace while the host sees different host PIDs. Those numbers are namespace-relative identities, not evidence of two host init processes. When debugging, establish which view a tool is showing. For isolation, pair namespace choices with appropriate permissions, resource controls, and careful handling of mounts and inherited descriptors.

cgroups.title: Account and constrain related work
cgroups.body: Control groups organize processes hierarchically and apply resource controllers. CPU controls can weight service or limit runtime; memory controls can define pressure and hard limits. A child's effective resources remain constrained by ancestors. Namespaces change what a process sees, while cgroups affect accounting and service; one does not replace the other.

cgroups.title: Example: idle host, throttled container
cgroups.body: A container can exhaust its CPU quota during a period and wait despite idle host capacity outside its allocation. Adding threads inside the container does not remove that cap. Inspect throttling and configured limits before increasing worker count. For memory, distinguish high-pressure events from hard-limit failure and examine whether the active working set fits the effective hierarchy.

container-file-systems.title: Layers and writable state
container-file-systems.body: Container images commonly use layered filesystems with a writable layer for runtime changes. Reading unchanged image data differs from modifying it, which may require copying an object into the writable layer. Volumes and bind mounts provide other storage paths with distinct ownership and lifetime. Deleting a name in an upper layer does not necessarily erase bytes from an immutable lower image layer.

container-file-systems.title: Example: editing a large image file
container-file-systems.body: A container modifies a small part of a large file inherited from an image. Copy-up behavior can create more I/O and storage use than the small application write suggests, depending on implementation. Place mutable datasets on an appropriate persistent storage path and measure its actual guarantees. Container recreation can remove the writable layer, so it is not an implicit backup strategy.

pid-1-and-signal-handling.title: The first process has lifecycle duties
pid-1-and-signal-handling.body: The process occupying PID 1 in a PID namespace has special responsibilities and signal behavior. It may need to reap adopted children and coordinate termination. A shell wrapper that does not forward signals can prevent the real application from seeing a graceful shutdown request. Container exit semantics also depend on the lifetime of its initial process.

pid-1-and-signal-handling.title: Example: shutdown reaches the wrapper
pid-1-and-signal-handling.body: A runtime sends a termination signal to a wrapper shell, but the server running beneath it never receives it. After a grace period the container is forcibly stopped, losing in-flight work. Use an appropriate exec-form startup or a suitable init/supervision arrangement, and test child reaping and signal forwarding. A healthy request path does not establish correct shutdown behavior.

container-resource-failures.title: Limits change failure modes
container-resource-failures.body: CPU limits can throttle work; memory limits can trigger reclaim or termination; process limits can prevent new threads or children. Descriptor and filesystem limits add other constraints. A generic application error may reflect any of these boundaries. Correlate the failure timestamp with resource events and effective ancestor limits instead of assuming the host's total capacity describes the container's allowance.

container-resource-failures.title: Example: threads fail before the heap is full
container-resource-failures.body: A service creates one thread per connection and eventually cannot create more threads. Heap usage may still look modest because task limits, stack reservations, or other resources are exhausted first. Bound concurrency and inspect task counts, stack configuration, and cgroup events. Raising only the heap ceiling may increase contention without addressing the actual limiting resource.

container-security.title: Reduce authority across several layers
container-security.body: Container isolation combines namespaces, resource controls, credentials, capability restrictions, syscall filtering, and filesystem choices. A privileged container or sensitive host mount can undermine expected boundaries. Images also bring dependencies and application vulnerabilities. Decide which resources the workload truly needs and reduce unnecessary access; the presence of a container runtime is not itself a complete security policy.

container-security.title: Example: a powerful host socket
container-security.body: Mounting a host management socket into an otherwise restricted container can expose authority far beyond its visible filesystem. Evaluate the operations available through each mounted endpoint and descriptor, not just file paths. Run with suitable identities, minimize capabilities, protect secrets, and keep the host kernel maintained. A read-only root filesystem helps some risks but does not constrain every external capability.

a-systematic-debugging-method.title: Turn symptoms into falsifiable hypotheses
a-systematic-debugging-method.body: Start with the user-visible failure and its time interval. Record what changed, define competing explanations, and choose a measurement that distinguishes them. CPU, memory, storage, network, and locks are connected, so one abnormal counter may be a consequence rather than a cause. Preserve a baseline and change one controlled variable where practical.

a-systematic-debugging-method.title: Example: slow API with low CPU
a-systematic-debugging-method.body: Possible causes include a slow dependency, lock contention, storage waits, or a concurrency limit. An on-CPU profile alone cannot separate all of them. Measure request-stage timings and waiting states, then inspect the implicated dependency. If a hypothesis predicts long database time but traces show fast database calls, revise it rather than collecting more unrelated CPU screenshots.

investigating-processes.title: Establish identity and relationships
investigating-processes.body: Identify the process, its parent and children, start time, command, credentials, and relevant namespace. A PID can be reused after exit, so historical observations need timestamps and identity context. Inspect task states and thread counts rather than treating the process as one undifferentiated activity. Supervisors and wrappers may be the visible process without doing the actual request work.

investigating-processes.title: Example: restarting the wrong worker
investigating-processes.body: A service has a parent supervisor and several children. One child grows memory while the parent remains small. Monitoring only the parent misses the problem, and restarting an unrelated PID may affect another workload. Correlate ownership, lifetime, and per-child metrics. Inspect repeated growth after controlled restarts to distinguish persistent workload demand from an instance-specific leak.

investigating-cpu.title: Utilization and runnable delay differ
investigating-cpu.body: CPU utilization reports execution time, while runnable delay measures waiting to execute. A process can be constrained by affinity or quota even when the host has idle CPUs. Separate user and kernel work, and use a profile to attribute on-CPU cost. High utilization can be healthy productive throughput; it becomes a problem relative to latency and capacity objectives.

investigating-cpu.title: Example: one saturated event loop
investigating-cpu.body: A service uses one event-loop thread on a many-core host. Overall utilization looks low, but its single thread consumes a full CPU and queues requests. Inspect per-thread CPU and request delay. Optimize the hot path or distribute suitable work; increasing the number of accepted connections merely enlarges the queue unless execution capacity also changes.

investigating-memory.title: Distinguish retained objects from retained pages
investigating-memory.body: Application allocations, allocator caches, mapped files, and shared resident pages contribute differently to memory reports. Track a time series and relate it to workload phases. A rising RSS can represent useful warm caches or a leak. A heap profile explains managed objects but may omit native buffers, thread stacks, mappings, and kernel resources attributed elsewhere.

investigating-memory.title: Example: growth after traffic stops
investigating-memory.body: After a load test, live object counts return to baseline but RSS stays elevated. The allocator may retain free arenas for future use. If live retained objects also keep increasing across repeated cycles, investigate ownership paths. Compare equivalent workload cycles and use the right metric before declaring either a leak or harmless caching solely from one memory snapshot.

investigating-disk.title: Separate capacity, service time, and access pattern
investigating-disk.body: Disk-full errors, high device latency, metadata contention, and durability waits require different fixes. Observe filesystem free space and inode availability alongside request size, queueing, and latency. Caches can hide device work temporarily. Network-backed storage adds another layer, so device statistics on the local host may not capture the true backend bottleneck.

investigating-disk.title: Example: free bytes but failed creates
investigating-disk.body: A filesystem can have free byte capacity while exhausting another required resource such as inodes or a quota. Deleting a few huge files may not address a workload producing millions of tiny files. Inspect the actual error and relevant counters. Test a representative operation instead of relying on a generic throughput benchmark that never creates the same metadata pressure.

investigating-system-calls.title: Trace boundaries without confusing them with causes
investigating-system-calls.body: A syscall trace shows operations, arguments, results, and timing at the user/kernel boundary. It can expose repeated missing-file lookups, short I/O, and long waits. It does not explain all user-space computation, and tracing changes timing. Narrow the process, duration, and operations to the question; captured arguments can also contain sensitive application data.

investigating-system-calls.title: Example: repeated failing opens
investigating-system-calls.body: A process tries several nonexistent configuration paths for every request. Tracing reveals the repeated failures even though individual calls are fast. Caching a valid configuration path or correcting initialization can remove the repeated work. Validate the improvement with end-to-end latency and workload volume; a large count of cheap syscalls may matter less than one slow dependency wait.

investigating-network-and-sockets.title: Inspect both transport and application progress
investigating-network-and-sockets.body: Socket state, queue sizes, connection counts, and retransmission observations help locate waiting. A connected TCP socket does not prove the application protocol is healthy. Growing send queues can reflect a slow reader or network problem; growing receive queues can reflect an application not consuming data. Correlate these observations with deadlines and request-stage timings.

investigating-network-and-sockets.title: Example: successful connect, no response
investigating-network-and-sockets.body: A client establishes TCP quickly but waits for the first application byte. The delay could be server queueing, backend work, TLS or protocol negotiation, or response buffering. Separate connection establishment from request and response timing. Increasing the connect timeout cannot fix a post-connect bottleneck, and retrying indiscriminately can amplify server overload.

file-descriptor-exhaustion.title: Each open reference needs a lifecycle
file-descriptor-exhaustion.body: Files, sockets, pipes, and event interfaces can all consume descriptors. Per-process limits and broader system constraints differ. A leak often occurs on uncommon errors or cancellations rather than the happy path. Count descriptors by type and compare their growth with active work. Descriptor number reuse also makes stale callbacks dangerous after a resource closes.

file-descriptor-exhaustion.title: Example: failed connections leak sockets
file-descriptor-exhaustion.body: A connection succeeds or fails, but cleanup closes the descriptor only on success. During an outage, repeated failures accumulate descriptors until unrelated opens and accepts fail. Put cleanup under explicit ownership so every path closes exactly once. Reproduce cancellation and timeout paths as well as normal completion; increasing limits alone hides the leak temporarily.

profiling-and-flame-graphs.title: Sampling answers a specific time question
profiling-and-flame-graphs.body: An on-CPU profile samples executing stacks; a flame graph aggregates stack presence rather than displaying a chronological call sequence. Wide frames indicate accumulated sampled cost in the selected view. Off-CPU or allocation profiles answer different questions. Sampling frequency, symbol quality, inlining, and missing stacks can all affect interpretation, so inspect collection conditions before drawing precise conclusions.

profiling-and-flame-graphs.title: Example: a wide waiting function
profiling-and-flame-graphs.body: A wall-time or off-CPU view may show a blocking function as wide while an on-CPU profile barely shows it. Neither is necessarily wrong; they measure different time. Optimize the relevant critical path and remeasure under comparable load. Removing a narrow CPU function cannot materially reduce a request dominated by remote waiting, even if that function appears in every request.

ebpf-and-bpftrace.title: Observe selected kernel and user events
ebpf-and-bpftrace.body: eBPF-based tooling can attach bounded programs to supported observation points, aggregate events, and report selected data with less overhead than exporting every event. Verification and attachment constraints reduce certain risks but do not make all tracing free. Kernel version, permissions, symbols, and event availability affect which probes work. Begin with a precise question and a bounded observation window.

ebpf-and-bpftrace.title: Example: a latency distribution
ebpf-and-bpftrace.body: Instead of printing every I/O event, aggregate operation durations into a histogram keyed by a small, controlled set of categories. This reveals a long tail without generating enormous logs. Validate units, start/end correlation, and missed events before trusting the distribution. High-cardinality keys can consume substantial map memory, and missing completions can bias results unless explicitly accounted for.
